#!/bin/sh
# Run a bundled lesson through a loopback mlpl-serve session and print its recording under the peer version-zero schema.
# usage: capture-recording <demo.mlpl> <lesson-slug> <max_frames> <max_observations_per_frame> <max_values_per_observation> <max_total_values>
set -eu

repo_root=$(CDPATH= cd -- "$(dirname -- "$0")/.." && pwd)
[ "$#" -eq 6 ] || { echo "usage: capture-recording <demo> <lesson> <frames> <obs/frame> <values/obs> <total values>" >&2; exit 1; }
demo=$1; lesson=$2; max_frames=$3; max_obs=$4; max_values=$5; max_total=$6
server=$("$repo_root/scripts/select-mlpl-serve")
port=${MOE_RECORD_PORT:-16493}
base_url="http://127.0.0.1:$port"
log_file=$(mktemp)
response_file=$(mktemp)
program_file=$(mktemp)

cleanup() {
    if [ -n "${server_pid:-}" ]; then
        kill "$server_pid" 2>/dev/null || true
        wait "$server_pid" 2>/dev/null || true
    fi
    rm -f "$log_file" "$response_file" "$program_file"
}
trap cleanup EXIT HUP INT TERM

command -v curl >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "curl is required" >&2; exit 1; }
command -v jq >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "jq is required" >&2; exit 1; }

"$repo_root/scripts/bundle-program" "$repo_root/$demo" > "$program_file"

"$server" --bind "127.0.0.1:$port" --auth disabled >"$log_file" 2>&1 &
server_pid=$!
attempt=0
until curl --fail --silent "$base_url/v1/health" >/dev/null 2>&1; do
    attempt=$((attempt + 1))
    if [ "$attempt" -ge 50 ] || ! kill -0 "$server_pid" 2>/dev/null; then
        echo "mlpl-serve did not become ready" >&2
        sed -n '1,20p' "$log_file" >&2
        exit 1
    fi
    sleep 0.1
done

session=$(curl --fail --silent --request POST "$base_url/v1/sessions")
session_id=$(printf '%s' "$session" | jq -r '.session_id')
token=$(printf '%s' "$session" | jq -r '.token')
body=$(jq -nc --rawfile program "$program_file" '{program: $program}')

curl --fail --silent --no-buffer \
    --header "Authorization: Bearer $token" \
    --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    --data "$body" \
    "$base_url/v1/sessions/$session_id/eval_stream" >"$response_file"

if sed -n 's/^event: *//p' "$response_file" | grep -q '^error$'; then
    echo "server run reported an error: $(sed -n 's/^data: *//p' "$response_file" | tail -1)" >&2
    exit 1
fi

sed -n 's/^data: *//p' "$response_file" | jq -s \
    --arg lesson "$lesson" --argjson f "$max_frames" --argjson o "$max_obs" --argjson v "$max_values" --argjson t "$max_total" '
  [ .[] | select(.name != null and .shape != null) | {step, observation: {name, shape, values}} ]
  | group_by(.step)
  | map({step: .[0].step, observations: map(.observation)})
  | {
      schema: "sw-ml-study.ml-microscope-recording",
      version: 0,
      lesson: $lesson,
      budgets: {max_frames: $f, max_observations_per_frame: $o, max_values_per_observation: $v, max_total_values: $t},
      frames: .
    }
'

    }

    echo "PASS probe $name resolved upstream: $pattern"
}

=== 28478d6
RM01: the mixture block applied R times with re-routing, and finding F23

The MX01 block (attention, four routed experts, balance term) is applied
R times to the same token state with deep supervision; the router runs at
every recurrence and the balance term is applied per recurrence. One
process per R (finding F22), R = 2 and R = 3, the R = 3 run recorded over
the live server and replayed in the live demo as lesson rm01.

Results (rows RM01@2 and RM01@3): 38 to 46 percent of tokens change
expert between consecutive recurrences; the R = 3 mixture reaches
validation loss 3.42 (the lowest of any 120-example model in the table)
with training exact match 0.43; R = 2 is worse than MX01 (4.09).
Specialization 0.65 at the first recurrence, 0.45 and 0.49 after it.
Three diagrams (strip, loads per recurrence, family maps per
recurrence) composed by a drawer from the committed metrics.

Finding F23: a reshape whose row count is derived from shape() inside
grad drops the gradient through the reshaped value without an error. The
first R = 2 run collapsed onto expert 0 (loads 406, 0, 0, 0). Pinned by
probes/f23_shape_derived_reshape_in_grad.mlpl and scripts/run-probes;
filed in the findings, blockers, and cross-repo handoffs. Workaround:
literal window length, prompts padded to it.

Also carried here: the F16 resolution flip in scripts/run-emit-frame-loops
(bare include refused, nested includes resolve rooted at the map,
parent-relative refused), finding 9 (recurrence) in current-findings, the
recurrence concept page, README and live page updated for the two new
recordings and the recur and rm recipes.

#!/bin/sh
set -eu

repo_dir=$(CDPATH= cd -- "$(dirname -- "$0")/.." && pwd)
status=0

for file in "$repo_dir"/README.md "$repo_dir"/docs/*.md "$repo_dir"/docs/*/*.md; do
    targets=$(sed -n 's/.*](\([^):#][^)]*\)).*/\1/p' "$file")
    for target in $targets; do
        target=${target%%#*}
        [ -z "$target" ] && continue
        case "$target" in
            ../*|http://*|https://*) continue ;;
        esac
        base=$(dirname -- "$file")
        if [ ! -e "$base/$target" ]; then
            echo "broken local link in ${file#"$repo_dir/"}: $target" >&2
            status=1
        fi
    done
done

[ "$status" -eq 0 ] && echo "PASS documentation links"
exit "$status"

## Build and run

Prerequisites:

- the adjacent [`../sw-mlpl`](https://github.com/sw-ml-study/sw-mlpl) checkout built in release mode

- [`just`](https://github.com/casey/just);
- `agentrail` for the development process.

The scripts only select existing tools; they never install or overwrite them.

```sh
just                 # list recipes
just check           # the complete pre-commit gate
just tests           # native mlplunit tests (arguments filter paths or tags)
just probes          # re-run the upstream-finding reproducers
just domain          # run DM01 and check its diagrams
just dense           # run DN01 (about 16 s) and check its diagrams and results row
just teacher         # validate the committed TE01 fixture without retraining

just delta           # run LD01 low-rank delta experts with a shared FFN (about 80 s)

just benchmark       # GB01 generation benchmark fixture and document (write to re-measure)
just mlpl-style      # canonical formatting and docstring checks
```

`just check` validates repository structure, documentation links,
peer-identical license files, the generated Agentrail briefing, MLPL style,
the native test suites, the pinned reproducers, and the DM01 and DN01 lessons
with their diagrams and results row (about half a minute in total). Each lesson extends the
gate with its own demo run, preview freshness check, recording check, and
catalog check.

The interactive host is the generic Rust/Yew/WASM microscope and MLPL web
framework in `../demo-extensions`; that Rust code is the only part of this
effort subject to `sw-checklist`.

Work is divided into durable Agentrail steps. In each fresh session run
`agentrail next`, then `agentrail begin`; implement only that step; run focused
tests and `just check`; commit source and `.agentrail/` metadata by name; push
`main`; and only then run `agentrail complete`. [`AGENTS.md`](AGENTS.md) holds
the full repository protocol and `CLAUDE.md` links to it.

  behavior lives in `scripts/`; do not add a Makefile.

=== arch 116-160
## Two execution paths, one semantics

Training uses a dense-masked formulation: every expert is evaluated and the
top-k gate zeroes the rest. The cost is dense but the mathematics is exactly
the sparse model, and autograd stays simple. Inference uses sparse dispatch:
only selected experts are evaluated, counted, cached, and scheduled. Every
lesson that introduces the sparse path asserts parity with the dense-masked
path on the same fixture. Systems measurements (expert evaluations, bytes,
hits, misses, q-star splits) come from the sparse path; quality measurements
come from either, since they agree.

## Scale tiers

The microscope scale (CPU, seconds, tens of thousands of parameters) is the
acceptance scale. The lab scale (MLX, minutes, millions of parameters) is
opt-in and uses the same source under `device("mlx") { }`. The embedded target
(256 MB, 0.5 TOPS) is an inference target for the packed file and is reached
by a later runtime handoff, not by this repository's interpreter path.

## Visual and measurement contract

Every step, data structure, and transformation has an annotated diagram that
states what it is, why it exists, and how it is computed, generated from the
same recorded values the tests assert on. Every lesson records memory, speed,
and quality in the catalog and the results table. The full contract is in the
[delivery plan](plan.md).

## Delivery boundary

This repository implements `.mlpl` model code, lessons, generators, oracles,
simulators, tests, fixtures, previews, and lesson text.

`../demo-mlpl-libraries` may later own domain-neutral helpers (observation
facade, byte packing, quantization arithmetic) after three unrelated consumers
prove them; consumption is by immutable revision and hash lock.

`../demo-extensions` owns the preferred generic Rust/Yew/WASM microscope host
and the optional native renderer. Its Rust work is subject to `sw-checklist`.

`../sw-mlpl` changes only for a measured language-wide gap with a minimal
executable reproducer, recorded first in the
[capability ledger](../reference/sw-mlpl-blockers.md).

## Explicit non-boundaries

acceptance scale. The lab scale (MLX, minutes, millions of parameters) is
opt-in and uses the same source under `device("mlx") { }`. The embedded target
(256 MB, 0.5 TOPS) is an inference target for the packed file and is reached
by a later runtime handoff, not by this repository's interpreter path.

## Visual and measurement contract

Every step, data structure, and transformation has an annotated diagram that
states what it is, why it exists, and how it is computed, generated from the
same recorded values the tests assert on. Every lesson records memory, speed,
and quality in the catalog and the results table. The full contract is in the
[delivery plan](plan.md).

## Delivery boundary

This repository implements `.mlpl` model code, lessons, generators, oracles,
simulators, tests, fixtures, previews, and lesson text.

`../demo-mlpl-libraries` may later own domain-neutral helpers (observation
facade, byte packing, quantization arithmetic) after three unrelated consumers
prove them; consumption is by immutable revision and hash lock.

`../demo-extensions` owns the preferred generic Rust/Yew/WASM microscope host
and the optional native renderer. Its Rust work is subject to `sw-checklist`.

`../sw-mlpl` changes only for a measured language-wide gap with a minimal
executable reproducer, recorded first in the
[capability ledger](../reference/sw-mlpl-blockers.md).

## Explicit non-boundaries

#!/bin/sh
# Gate cache, sourced by the demo gate scripts: a check run whose inputs are byte-identical to a
# previous passing check run prints "PASS <script> (cached)" and exits 0 instead of retraining.
#
# Usage inside a gate script (after repo_root and mode are set):
#
#   . "$repo_root/scripts/gate-cache"
#   gate_cache_start "$mode" run-dense-demo demos/dense_baseline.mlpl \
#       assets/previews/dense-run.svg "row:docs/reference/results.md:| DN01 |" conf:DN01
#   ... the run and its comparisons, exiting non-zero on any failure ...
#   gate_cache_record "$mode"
#   echo "PASS ..."
#
# Loops that cache one entry per item use the pieces: gate_cache_key NAME SPEC..., then
# gate_cache_hit MODE (true on a usable entry), then gate_cache_record MODE after the item passes.
#
# Input specs, paths relative to the repository root:
#   PATH            a file (hashed) or a directory (every file under it, sorted). A .mlpl file
#                   also contributes its transitive include closure and every fixtures/, docs/,
#                   assets/, or catalog/ path literal those sources name.
#   row:FILE:TEXT   the lines of FILE that contain TEXT (one lesson's results rows)
#   conf:ID         the scripts/recordings.conf line for lesson ID
#   bin:PATH        an absolute path to an executable, hashed as bytes (mlpl-serve has no --version)
#   text:STRING     a literal
# Always included: the calling script, this file, and the selected mlpl-repl's version and
# commit lines. The key is the sha256 of the sorted manifest; the entry file holds the manifest.
#
# Environment: GATE_FRESH=1 ignores existing entries (a passing run still records one);
# GATE_CACHE_DIR overrides tmp/gate-cache. Write mode never reads or records the cache, so the
# first check after a write reruns the lesson against the files the write installed.

gate_cache_dir=${GATE_CACHE_DIR:-$repo_root/tmp/gate-cache}
gate_key=""
gate_name=""
gate_manifest=""

gate_sha() {
    shasum -a 256 "$1" | awk '{ print $1 }'
}

gate_rel() {
    case "$1" in
        "$repo_root"/*) printf '%s\n' "${1#"$repo_root"/}" ;;
        *) printf '%s\n' "$1" ;;
    esac
}

# Print the absolute path of $1 and, recursively, every file it includes; $2 is the chain guarding cycles.
gate_includes() {
    _gi_file=$1
    _gi_chain=${2:-}
    case " $_gi_chain " in *" $_gi_file "*) return 0 ;; esac
    printf '%s\n' "$_gi_file"
    _gi_dir=$(dirname -- "$_gi_file")
    for _gi_target in $(sed -n 's/^include "\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' "$_gi_file"); do
        _gi_path=$(CDPATH= cd -- "$_gi_dir" && cd -- "$(dirname -- "$_gi_target")" && pwd)/$(basename -- "$_gi_target")
        gate_includes "$_gi_path" "$_gi_chain $_gi_file"
    done
}

# Print "file REL SHA" for a file, or for every file under a directory.
gate_hash_path() {
    if [ -d "$1" ]; then
        find "$1" -type f | LC_ALL=C sort | while IFS= read -r _hp_file; do
            printf 'file %s %s\n' "$(gate_rel "$_hp_file")" "$(gate_sha "$_hp_file")"
        done
    elif [ -f "$1" ]; then
        printf 'file %s %s\n' "$(gate_rel "$1")" "$(gate_sha "$1")"
    else
        printf 'missing %s\n' "$(gate_rel "$1")"
    fi
}

# Print the manifest lines for one spec.
gate_spec_lines() {
    _sl_spec=$1
    case "$_sl_spec" in
        row:*)
            _sl_rest=${_sl_spec#row:}
            _sl_file=${_sl_rest%%:*}
            _sl_text=${_sl_rest#*:}
            _sl_sha=$(grep -F -- "$_sl_text" "$repo_root/$_sl_file" 2>/dev/null | shasum -a 256 | awk '{ print $1 }')
            printf 'row %s %s %s\n' "$_sl_file" "$_sl_text" "$_sl_sha"
            ;;
        conf:*)
            _sl_id=${_sl_spec#conf:}
            _sl_sha=$(grep -- "^$_sl_id|" "$repo_root/scripts/recordings.conf" 2>/dev/null | shasum -a 256 | awk '{ print $1 }')
            printf 'conf %s %s\n' "$_sl_id" "$_sl_sha"
            ;;
        bin:*)
            _sl_bin=${_sl_spec#bin:}
            printf 'bin %s %s\n' "$_sl_bin" "$(gate_sha "$_sl_bin")"
            ;;
        text:*)
            printf 'text %s\n' "${_sl_spec#text:}"
            ;;
        *)
            case "$_sl_spec" in
                /*) _sl_abs=$_sl_spec ;;
                *) _sl_abs=$repo_root/$_sl_spec ;;
            esac
            case "$_sl_abs" in
                *.mlpl)
                    _sl_closure=$(gate_includes "$_sl_abs" | LC_ALL=C sort -u)
                    for _sl_src in $_sl_closure; do
                        gate_hash_path "$_sl_src"
                    done
                    for _sl_lit in $(printf '%s\n' "$_sl_closure" | xargs grep -o -h -E '"(fixtures|docs|assets|catalog)/[^"]*"' 2>/dev/null | tr -d '"' | LC_ALL=C sort -u); do
                        [ -e "$repo_root/$_sl_lit" ] && gate_hash_path "$repo_root/$_sl_lit"
                    done
                    ;;
                *) gate_hash_path "$_sl_abs" ;;
            esac
            ;;
    esac
}

# Compute gate_key and gate_manifest for NAME over the given specs.
gate_cache_key() {
    gate_name=$1
    shift
    _ck_mlpl=$("$repo_root/scripts/select-mlpl")
    _ck_self=$(CDPATH= cd -- "$(dirname -- "$0")" && pwd)/$(basename -- "$0")
    gate_manifest=$(
        printf 'mlpl %s\n' "$("$_ck_mlpl" --version 2>/dev/null | awk 'NR == 1 || /Commit:/ { gsub(/^[ \t]+/, ""); printf "%s ", $0 } END { print "" }')"
        gate_hash_path "$_ck_self"
        gate_hash_path "$repo_root/scripts/gate-cache"
        for _ck_spec in "$@"; do
            gate_spec_lines "$_ck_spec"
        done
    )
    gate_manifest=$(printf '%s\n' "$gate_manifest" | LC_ALL=C sort -u)
    gate_key=$(printf '%s\n' "$gate_manifest" | shasum -a 256 | awk '{ print $1 }')
}

# True when MODE is check, the cache is not bypassed, and the current key has a recorded pass.
gate_cache_hit() {
    [ "$1" = "check" ] || return 1
    case "${GATE_FRESH:-}" in ''|0) ;; *) return 1 ;; esac
    [ -n "$gate_key" ] && [ -f "$gate_cache_dir/$gate_name/$gate_key" ]
}

# Record the current key as passed when MODE is check.
gate_cache_record() {
    [ "$1" = "check" ] || return 0
    [ -n "$gate_key" ] || return 0
    mkdir -p "$gate_cache_dir/$gate_name"
    printf '%s\n' "$gate_manifest" > "$gate_cache_dir/$gate_name/$gate_key.tmp.$$"
    mv "$gate_cache_dir/$gate_name/$gate_key.tmp.$$" "$gate_cache_dir/$gate_name/$gate_key"
}

# Convenience for single-entry scripts: compute the key and exit 0 with a PASS line on a hit.
gate_cache_start() {
    _cs_mode=$1
    shift
    gate_cache_key "$@"
    if gate_cache_hit "$_cs_mode"; then
        echo "PASS $gate_name (cached)"
        exit 0
    fi
}

#!/bin/sh
# Prove that live mlpl-serve runs reproduce the committed recordings exactly; each lesson has its own gate-cache entry. usage: run-recording-parity [check|write] [ID ...] (default: every configured lesson)
set -eu

repo_root=$(CDPATH= cd -- "$(dirname -- "$0")/.." && pwd)
mode=${1:-check}
[ "$#" -gt 0 ] && shift
wanted="$*"
server=$("$repo_root/scripts/select-mlpl-serve")
. "$repo_root/scripts/gate-cache"

while IFS='|' read -r id lesson demo recording preview mf mo mv mt first last; do
    case "$id" in ''|\#*) continue ;; esac
    if [ -n "$wanted" ]; then
        case " $wanted " in *" $id "*) ;; *) continue ;; esac
    fi
    gate_cache_key "run-recording-parity-$id" "$demo" "$recording" "conf:$id" \
        scripts/capture-recording scripts/bundle-program scripts/select-mlpl-serve "bin:$server"
    if gate_cache_hit "$mode"; then
        echo "PASS run-recording-parity-$id (cached)"
        continue
    fi
    actual=$("$repo_root/scripts/capture-recording" "$demo" "$lesson" "$mf" "$mo" "$mv" "$mt")
    if [ "$mode" = "write" ]; then
        printf '%s\n' "$actual" > "$repo_root/$recording"
        echo "wrote $recording"
    elif [ "$(printf '%s' "$actual" | jq -S -c .)" != "$(jq -S -c . "$repo_root/$recording")" ]; then
        echo "live $id recording differs from the committed fixture; run scripts/run-recording-parity write $id" >&2
        exit 1
    else
        gate_cache_record "$mode"
        echo "PASS live $id SSE recording matches the committed fixture"
    fi
done < "$repo_root/scripts/recordings.conf"
if [ "$mode" = "write" ]; then
    "$repo_root/scripts/make-recording-index"
fi

# records nothing; write mode and GATE_FRESH=1 never use the cache; the manifest lists transitive includes, path literals,
# rows, and the recordings.conf line. The two lessons run are DM01 and the routing microscope (well under a second each).
set -eu

MLPL=$("$repo_root/scripts/select-mlpl")
export MLPL
work=$(mktemp -d "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/gate-cache-test.XXXXXX")
trap 'rm -rf "$work"' EXIT HUP INT TERM
copy="$work/repo"
for dir in lib demos scripts fixtures assets/previews docs/reference; do
    mkdir -p "$copy/$(dirname -- "$dir")"
    cp -R "$repo_root/$dir" "$copy/$dir"
done
GATE_CACHE_DIR="$work/cache"
export GATE_CACHE_DIR
unset GATE_FRESH

fail() { echo "gate cache test: $1" >&2; exit 1; }

# run NAME [ARGS...]: run the copied script, remember its output and status.
run() {
    name=$1
    shift
    if output=$("$copy/scripts/$name" "$@" 2>&1); then status=0; else status=$?; fi
}
expect_ran() { [ "$status" -eq 0 ] || fail "$1 failed: $output"; case "$output" in *"(cached)"*) fail "$1 was served from the cache but $2" ;; esac; }
expect_cached() { [ "$status" -eq 0 ] || fail "$1 failed: $output"; case "$output" in *"(cached)"*) ;; *) fail "$1 reran but $2" ;; esac; }
expect_failed() { [ "$status" -ne 0 ] || fail "$1 passed but $2"; }
entries() { find "$GATE_CACHE_DIR/$1" -type f 2>/dev/null | wc -l | tr -d ' '; }

run run-domain-demo; expect_ran run-domain-demo "the cache was empty"
run run-router-demo; expect_ran run-router-demo "the cache was empty"
[ "$(entries run-domain-demo)" = 1 ] && [ "$(entries run-router-demo)" = 1 ] || fail "a passing check run did not record one entry each"

run run-domain-demo; expect_cached run-domain-demo "nothing changed"
run run-router-demo; expect_cached run-router-demo "nothing changed"

run run-router-demo write; expect_ran "run-router-demo write" "write mode never uses the cache"
[ "$(entries run-router-demo)" = 1 ] || fail "write mode recorded an entry"
GATE_FRESH=1 run run-router-demo; expect_ran "GATE_FRESH=1 run-router-demo" "GATE_FRESH must bypass it"

run run-router-demo; expect_ran run-router-demo "lib/moe.mlpl, which it includes, changed"
run run-domain-demo; expect_cached run-domain-demo "lib/moe.mlpl is not in its include closure"
[ "$(entries run-router-demo)" = 2 ] || fail "the rerun after the library edit did not record a second key"

run run-router-demo; expect_ran run-router-demo "lib/svg.mlpl changed"
run run-domain-demo; expect_ran run-domain-demo "lib/svg.mlpl changed"

# A stale committed preview must fail the check and record nothing.
cp "$copy/assets/previews/router-routing.svg" "$work/router-routing.svg"
printf '<!-- stale -->\n' >> "$copy/assets/previews/router-routing.svg"
before=$(entries run-router-demo)
run run-router-demo; expect_failed run-router-demo "its committed preview is stale"
[ "$(entries run-router-demo)" = "$before" ] || fail "a failing run recorded an entry"
cp "$work/router-routing.svg" "$copy/assets/previews/router-routing.svg"
run run-router-demo; expect_cached run-router-demo "the preview is back to the recorded content"

# The manifest names transitive includes, path literals, results rows, and the recordings.conf line.
manifest=$(
    cd "$copy" && repo_root=$copy && . "$copy/scripts/gate-cache" &&

    printf '%s\n' "$gate_manifest"
)
for needle in "file lib/dense.mlpl" "file lib/domain.mlpl" "file lib/evaluate.mlpl" "file fixtures/domain/mixture-v0.json" \

done
case "$manifest" in *"lib/moe.mlpl"*) fail "manifest for the dense baseline names lib/moe.mlpl, which it does not include" ;; esac
key_before=$(printf '%s\n' "$manifest" | shasum -a 256 | awk '{ print $1 }')

    cd "$copy" && repo_root=$copy && . "$copy/scripts/gate-cache" &&
    gate_cache_key probe demos/dense_baseline.mlpl "row:docs/reference/results.md:| DN01 |" conf:DN01 &&
    printf '%s\n' "$gate_manifest"
)
[ "$(printf '%s\n' "$manifest_after" | shasum -a 256 | awk '{ print $1 }')" != "$key_before" ] || fail "editing the DN01 row did not change the key"

echo "PASS gate cache keyed by source, include closure, fixtures, previews, rows, and conf (library edit reruns only dependents)"
SH

attachment.snippet:
1	#!/bin/sh
2	# Gate cache, sourced by the demo gate scripts: a check run whose inputs are byte-identical to a
3	# previous passing check run prints "PASS <script> (cached)" and exits 0 instead of retraining.
4	#
5	# Usage inside a gate script (after repo_root and mode are set):
6	#
7	#   . "$repo_root/scripts/gate-cache"
8	#   gate_cache_start "$mode" run-dense-demo demos/dense_baseline.mlpl \
9	#       assets/previews/dense-run.svg "row:docs/reference/results.md:| DN01 |" conf:DN01
10	#   ... the run and its comparisons, exiting non-zero on any failure ...
11	#   gate_cache_record "$mode"
12	#   echo "PASS ..."
13	#
14	# Loops that cache one entry per item use the pieces: gate_cache_key NAME SPEC..., then
15	# gate_cache_hit MODE (true on a usable entry), then gate_cache_record MODE after the item passes.
16	#
17	# Input specs, paths relative to the repository root:
18	#   PATH            a file (hashed) or a directory (every file under it, sorted). A .mlpl file
19	#                   also contributes its transitive include closure and every fixtures/, docs/,
20	#                   assets/, or catalog/ path literal those sources name.
21	#   row:FILE:TEXT   the lines of FILE that contain TEXT (one lesson's results rows)
22	#   conf:ID         the scripts/recordings.conf line for lesson ID
23	#   bin:PATH        an absolute path to an executable, hashed as bytes (mlpl-serve has no --version)
24	#   text:STRING     a literal
25	# Always included: the calling script, this file, and the selected mlpl-repl's version and
26	# commit lines. The key is the sha256 of the sorted manifest; the entry file holds the manifest.
27	#
28	# Environment: GATE_FRESH=1 ignores existing entries (a passing run still records one);
29	# GATE_CACHE_DIR overrides tmp/gate-cache. Write mode never reads or records the cache, so the
30	# first check after a write reruns the lesson against the files the write installed.
31	
32	gate_cache_dir=${GATE_CACHE_DIR:-$repo_root/tmp/gate-cache}
33	gate_root=$(CDPATH= cd -- "$repo_root" && pwd)
34	gate_key=""
35	gate_name=""
36	gate_manifest=""
37	
38	gate_sha() {
39	    shasum -a 256 "$1" | awk '{ print $1 }'
40	}
41	
42	gate_rel() {
43	    case "$1" in
44	        "$gate_root"/*) printf '%s\n' "${1#"$gate_root"/}" ;;
45	        *) printf '%s\n' "$1" ;;
46	    esac
47	}
48	
49	# Print the absolute path of $1 and, recursively, every file it includes; $2 is the chain guarding cycles.
50	gate_includes() {
51	    _gi_file=$1
52	    _gi_chain=${2:-}
53	    case " $_gi_chain " in *" $_gi_file "*) return 0 ;; esac
54	    printf '%s\n' "$_gi_file"
55	    _gi_dir=$(dirname -- "$_gi_file")
56	    for _gi_target in $(sed -n 's/^include "\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' "$_gi_file"); do
57	        _gi_path=$(CDPATH= cd -- "$_gi_dir" && cd -- "$(dirname -- "$_gi_target")" && pwd)/$(basename -- "$_gi_target")
58	        gate_includes "$_gi_path" "$_gi_chain $_gi_file"
59	    done
60	}
61	
62	# Print "file REL SHA" for a file, or for every file under a directory.
63	gate_hash_path() {
64	    if [ -d "$1" ]; then
65	        find "$1" -type f | LC_ALL=C sort | while IFS= read -r _hp_file; do
66	            printf 'file %s %s\n' "$(gate_rel "$_hp_file")" "$(gate_sha "$_hp_file")"
67	        done
68	    elif [ -f "$1" ]; then
69	        printf 'file %s %s\n' "$(gate_rel "$1")" "$(gate_sha "$1")"
70	    else
71	        printf 'missing %s\n' "$(gate_rel "$1")"
72	    fi
73	}
74	
75	# Print the manifest lines for one spec.
76	gate_spec_lines() {
77	    _sl_spec=$1
78	    case "$_sl_spec" in
79	        row:*)
80	            _sl_rest=${_sl_spec#row:}
81	            _sl_file=${_sl_rest%%:*}

content.thinking: Found the true root cause: the server runs inside a `( cd ... ) &` subshell, so the trap kills the subshell but orphans the Python process, which keeps holding the port for the next run. I'll fix this by starting Python directly with its directory flag instead of using a subshell.

input.command:
for p in $(lsof -t -i :8791); do kill $p; done; sleep 1; python3 - <<'PY'
import pathlib
p = pathlib.Path("scripts/check-landscape"); s = p.read_text()
old = """(cd "$site" && python3 -m http.server "$port" --bind 127.0.0.1 > /dev/null 2>&1) &
server=$!
"""
new = """# Started directly (no subshell) so the trap's kill reaches the server itself and cannot orphan it on the port.
python3 -m http.server "$port" --bind 127.0.0.1 --directory "$site" > /dev/null 2>&1 &
server=$!
"""
assert s.count(old) == 1; p.write_text(s.replace(old, new))
PY
for i in 1 2; do scripts/check-landscape > /dev/null 2>&1; echo "run $i exit $?"; done; lsof -nP -i :8791 || echo "port free after runs"

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

When an event lands that the user would want to act on now — an error appeared, the status they were waiting on flipped — send a PushNotification. Not every event is worth a push; the ones that change what they'd do next are.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

git add AGENTS.md README.md docs/implementation/README.md docs/overview/architecture.md justfile scripts/check scripts/check-docs scripts/check-gate-cache scripts/gate-cache scripts/check-landscape scripts/check-structure scripts/run-benchmark scripts/run-budget-demo scripts/run-campus-demo scripts/run-delta-demo scripts/run-dense-demo scripts/run-dispatch-demo scripts/run-docent-demo scripts/run-domain-demo scripts/run-engram-demo scripts/run-matcher-demo scripts/run-moe-demo scripts/run-moe2-demo scripts/run-re-demo scripts/run-recording-parity scripts/run-recur-demo scripts/run-rm-demo scripts/run-router-demo scripts/run-scale-sweep scripts/run-teacher scripts/run-walkthrough-export scripts/run-wordvec-demo .agentrail/steps/001-gate-cache/step.toml && git status --short | grep -v '^[MA] ' ; git commit -q -F - <<'MSG'
Gate cache: incremental just check keyed on content, plus just check-docs

Every demo gate script (scripts/run-*-demo, run-scale-sweep, run-benchmark,
run-teacher, run-walkthrough-export, run-recording-parity) now sources
scripts/gate-cache and computes a key before it runs: the sha256 of its demo
source, the library files it includes (transitively, following include
lines as bundle-program does), every fixtures/, docs/, assets/, or catalog/
path literal those sources name, the previews and fixtures it compares, the
results-table lines of its lessons, its recordings.conf line, the script
itself, the helper, and the mlpl binary's version and commit line
(run-recording-parity also hashes mlpl-serve and keeps one entry per
lesson). A check run whose key exists under tmp/gate-cache/<script>/ prints
PASS <script> (cached) and exits 0; a passing check run records its key
with the manifest it hashed; failing runs record nothing; write mode never
reads or records; just check --fresh (GATE_FRESH=1) ignores entries.

scripts/check-gate-cache proves the keying in a scratch copy with its own
cache directory and runs in the gate: a second run is cached, a library
edit reruns exactly the lessons whose include closure contains it, a stale
preview fails without recording, write mode and GATE_FRESH bypass the
cache, and the manifest names transitive includes, path literals, rows,
and the recordings line.

just check-docs runs structure, links, style, catalog, page, and landscape
only; AGENTS.md states when it is acceptable (no change under lib/, demos/,
tests/, probes/, scripts/run-*, fixtures/, or the binary).

Measured: the full gate from an empty cache 2495 s; the same gate with a
warm cache 51 s with 27 cached entries. A sibling rebuild of mlpl-repl
between two runs invalidated every entry, as the binary line intends.

Also fixed: check-landscape started its http.server inside a subshell, so
the exit trap killed the subshell and orphaned the server on the port; the
next run failed to bind, was served by the stale server, and exited 1
after printing PASS. The server now starts directly, the script fails
early if its own server is not alive, and the trap tolerates the reap.

content.text:
Step 001-gate-cache is complete, committed, pushed, and recorded. The worktree is clean.

**What landed** (commit 0dcf465, metadata in e556c48, both on `main`):

- **Content-keyed gate cache.** A sourced POSIX helper, `scripts/gate-cache`, is wired into all twenty single-entry demo gate scripts and into recording parity, which keeps one entry per lesson. The key hashes the demo source, its transitive include closure, every fixtures, docs, assets, or catalog path literal in those sources, the previews and fixtures compared, the lesson's results rows, its recordings.conf line, the script, the helper, and the interpreter's version and commit line. A check run with a recorded key prints `PASS <script> (cached)`. Failing runs record nothing, write mode never touches the cache, and `just check --fresh` or `GATE_FRESH=1` bypasses it.
- **Proof of keying.** A new test in the gate copies the sources to scratch space with its own cache directory and shows a library edit rerunning exactly the lessons that include it, a stale preview failing without recording, and write and fresh modes bypassing. It runs in about four seconds.
- **Documentation-only gate.** `just check-docs` runs structure, links, style, catalog, page, and landscape. AGENTS.md states it is acceptable only when nothing under lib, demos, tests, probes, run scripts, fixtures, or the binary changed. README, architecture, and the implementation index describe the mechanism.

**Measured timings**

| Run | Elapsed |
|---|---|
| Full gate, empty cache | 2495 s |
| Full gate, warm cache | 51 s (27 cached entries) |

A concurrent rebuild of the sibling interpreter between two runs invalidated every entry once, which is the binary line doing its job.

**Also fixed on the way.** The landscape check started its HTTP server in a subshell, so its exit trap orphaned the server on the port. Every later run failed to bind, was served by the stale process, and exited 1 after printing PASS. The server now starts directly and the script fails early if its own server is not alive.

**Flagged for a new step.** The emit-frame loops script has been a zero-byte file since the RM01 commit, so that gate probe passes trivially. I added step 008 to restore it rather than fixing it silently here.

**Next step** is 002-simple-ssm, the SS01 diagonal state-space block. Blockers: none.

#+title: mlplcode, a coding agent in sw-MLPL
#+subtitle: a literate reading of every MLPL file in the agent
#+author: Michael A Wright
#+startup: showall
#+property: header-args:mlpl :results output :exports code :eval no-export
#+property: header-args:text :eval never
#+property: header-args:emacs-lisp :eval no-export
#+options: toc:2 num:t

* How to read and run this document

This is the agent, in the order a reader should meet it, with prose before
every function. Each source block carries a ~:tangle~ target: tangling this
file regenerates the committed sources byte for byte, and ~just check~ runs
~scripts/check-tangle~ to prove it, so the prose can never describe code that
no longer exists. The committed ~.mlpl~ files remain the source of truth;
when they change, this document is edited to match.

** Evaluating blocks

The document never evaluates anything on export (~:eval no-export~ in the
header), so =C-c C-e h o= produces HTML with no prompts. Evaluation is for
reading interactively. To make =C-c C-c= work, evaluate this setup block
once per Emacs session; it loads sw-MLPL's org-babel backend from the
adjacent checkout and points it at whichever interpreter exists (GUI Emacs
has a minimal PATH, so the full path matters):

#+begin_src emacs-lisp :tangle no
(let* ((here (file-name-directory (buffer-file-name)))
       ;; The repository root is wherever AGENTS.md is, so this also works
       ;; on a copy of the document under out/ or work/.
       (repo (or (locate-dominating-file here "AGENTS.md") (expand-file-name ".." here)))
       (sw-mlpl (expand-file-name "../sw-mlpl" repo))
       (candidates (list (expand-file-name "target/release/mlpl-repl" sw-mlpl)
                         (expand-file-name "target/debug/mlpl-repl" sw-mlpl)
                         (executable-find "mlpl-repl")
                         (expand-file-name "~/.local/softwarewrighter/bin/mlpl-repl"))))
  (add-to-list 'load-path (expand-file-name "elisp" sw-mlpl))
  (require 'ob-mlpl)
  ;; Keep org-babel's scratch files inside the repository's ignored work/
  ;; directory rather than /tmp.
  (make-directory (expand-file-name "work" repo) t)
  (setq temporary-file-directory (expand-file-name "work/" repo))
  (setq org-babel-mlpl-command
        (or (seq-find (lambda (p) (and p (file-executable-p p))) candidates)
            (user-error "no mlpl-repl found; build ../sw-mlpl or set org-babel-mlpl-command")))
  (setq org-confirm-babel-evaluate nil)
  (message "ob-mlpl ready: %s" org-babel-mlpl-command))
#+end_src

Three things to know before pressing =C-c C-c= on a block:

- A block runs in a fresh interpreter on a temporary file, so a block that
  says ~include "model.mlpl"~ cannot find its neighbour and will report an
  include error. The function blocks in this document are for reading and
  tangling; the runnable ones are the small self-contained examples in the
  primer below.
- ~org-confirm-babel-evaluate~ controls the yes/no prompt. The setup block
  sets it to ~nil~ (never ask) for the session; set it back to ~t~ to be
  asked, or to a function to decide per block.

content.content:
Insert a new pending step at a chosen position, shifting later steps up

Use when a bug or unplanned task needs to slot in before existing pending work. The new step lands at position `after + 1`; every pending/in-progress step with a number greater than `after` shifts up by one (step.toml `number` and the on-disk `NNN-slug` directory name are both updated). The operation is refused if any step that would shift is already `Completed`, since completed steps anchor git-tracked history.

Pass `--after 0` to prepend at position 1 (only works if step 1 is pending).

Cursor semantic (preemption): if the new step lands at or before the current cursor, focus follows the new arrival — the inserted step becomes `current_step` and the previously focused step is pushed to `current_step + 1`. This matches the "drop in a blocker" use case. If the new step lands behind the cursor, focus is unchanged and the new step is queued as future work.

Usage: agentrail insert [OPTIONS] --after <AFTER> --slug <SLUG> --prompt <PROMPT>

Options:
      --after <AFTER>

Row SS02, diagrams (the selective gates on one window; SS01 against SS02 against DN01), docs/experiments/SS02.md, tests over the gates' dependence on the input, catalog and recording.

=== DN01.md
# DN01: dense baseline

## Question

How good is a tiny dense model on this domain, and what does every later
number compare against?

## Change from the previous experiment

The first model: one transformer block with a single feed-forward network.

## Configuration

Embedding width 16, hidden width 32, one head, causal attention with a
residual, RMS norm, an LM head; window 28; 120 examples; 300 epochs; Adam
at learning rate 0.003; masked cross-entropy over answer and stop tokens;
per-example training with no cross-example attention. About 16 seconds on
a laptop, deterministic, so diagrams and the results row are checked in
the gate.

## Results

| Metric | Value | Source |
|---|---:|---|
| Parameters | 3,812 | DN01 row |
| Active parameters per token | 2,996 | DN01 row |
| Bytes per token at f64 | 23,968 | DN01 row |
| Validation masked loss | 3.79 | DN01 row |
| Perplexity | 44.2 | DN01 row |
| Held-out exact match: arith / seq / mlpl / prose | 0 / 0 / 0 / 0.667 | DN01 row |
| Training exact match | 0.70 | dense-run diagram |
| Interpreter time per window | 0.020 ms | DN01 row |

![DN01 model: the example window through embedding, positions, residual attention, residual FFN, norm, head, and the argmax prediction beside the target](../../assets/previews/dense-model.svg)

![DN01 run: training and validation loss over 300 epochs, per-family exact-match bars, the attention heatmap of one example, and two decoded validation prompts](../../assets/previews/dense-run.svg)

## What we learned

At 120 examples the model memorizes: training loss keeps falling while
validation loss bottoms out and rises. Only prose generalizes. This is the
baseline for [finding 1](../results/current-findings.md).

## What we did not prove

That the dense model is capacity-limited; DS01 shows it is data-limited.

## Raw evidence

```sh
just dense           # run DN01 and check its diagrams and results row
just dense write     # regenerate the committed diagrams and the DN01 results row
```

content.content:
# State-space block

## What problem does it solve?

Attention carries context by keeping every earlier token's key and value,
so decode memory grows with the window and every new token reads all of
it. A state-space block (Mamba, Mamba-2) carries context in a fixed-size
state that is updated once per token and decays selectively: memory per
token is constant, and the block chooses, from the token itself, what to
keep and what to forget. NVIDIA's Nemotron-H and Nemotron 3 Nano interleave
such blocks with a few attention blocks and MoE feed-forward blocks, keeping
attention's exact recall where it matters and constant-memory context
everywhere else.

## Basic idea

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  x[token x_t] --> g[decay a_t and input b_t from x_t]
  h0[state h_t-1] --> u[h_t = a_t * h_t-1 + b_t * x_t]
  g --> u
  u --> o[output projection and gate]
  o --> y[y_t into the residual stream]
```

The selective scan written out: `h_t = a_t * h_(t-1) + b_t * x_t`, with
`a_t = sigmoid(x_t Wa)` (per-dimension decay in 0 to 1) and `b_t = x_t Wb`
(per-dimension input gate), then `y_t = h_t Wo` gated by the token. At
microscope scale the scan runs sequentially over the 28-position window;
`probes/c1_selective_scan_in_grad.mlpl` shows it traces through `grad`
and trains with `adam` today.

## What the microscope will measure

SS01: DN01 with attention replaced by the scan at matched parameters:
validation loss and family accuracy; the decay `a_t` per position on one
window (what the block forgets, drawn as a fading state chip); decode-time
bytes held per token for the state against the key-value cache attention
would hold, on the generation benchmark. SS02: the attention, state-space,
and MoE hybrid at several ratios, with the recurrence machinery for depth.

## What would demonstrate value

At matched parameters, the scan block within a small margin of attention's
validation loss with constant decode memory; and a hybrid ratio that keeps
attention's held-out MLPL answers (the first ones came from RC01 and RM01)
while the state-space blocks carry the rest at lower bytes per token.

## Status

Planned as Saga 7 (state-space-and-hybrid), next after the landscape:
SS01 simple, SS02 selective, HA01 with attention, SM01 with experts, LM01
latent experts. Nothing measured yet; the only evidence is the capability
probe.

## Deeper reference

- [Delivery plan](../overview/plan.md), Saga 7, and
  [`research4.txt`](../research/research4.txt)
- [Recurrence](recurrence.md) for the depth-without-parameters machinery
  the hybrid reuses
=== concepts README
# Concepts

A visual learning path. Each step adds one mechanism and asks one
question; each page answers what problem the mechanism solves, the basic
idea, what the microscope measures, what would demonstrate value, and
which experiments exist. Pages read front to back in this order.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[1 Dense model] --> B[2 Add experts]
  B --> C[3 Route to top-k]
  C --> D[4 Skip inactive experts]
  D --> E[5 Reuse one block recursively]
  E --> F[6 Add Engram memory]
  F --> G[7 Quantize experts]
  G --> H[8 Keep only hot experts resident]
  H --> I[9 Schedule across CPU and NPU]
```

| Step | Question | Page | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | How good is a tiny dense model? | [Dense versus MoE](dense-vs-moe.md) | measured (DN01) |
| 2, 3 | Can we store more model than we execute, and what does the second expert cost? | [Routing and top-k](routing.md) | measured (MX01, MX02) |
| 4 | Can conditional compute actually avoid the unused work? | [Sparse dispatch](sparse-dispatch.md) | measured (SD01, GB01) |

# State-space block

## What problem does it solve?

Attention carries context by keeping every earlier token's key and value,
so decode memory grows with the window and every new token reads all of
it. A state-space block (Mamba, Mamba-2) carries context in a fixed-size
state that is updated once per token and decays selectively: memory per
token is constant, and the block chooses, from the token itself, what to
keep and what to forget. NVIDIA's Nemotron-H and Nemotron 3 Nano interleave
such blocks with a few attention blocks and MoE feed-forward blocks, keeping
attention's exact recall where it matters and constant-memory context
everywhere else.

## Basic idea

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  x[token x_t] --> g[decay a_t and input b_t from x_t]
  h0[state h_t-1] --> u[h_t = a_t * h_t-1 + b_t * x_t]
  g --> u
  u --> o[output projection and gate]
  o --> y[y_t into the residual stream]
```

The selective scan written out: `h_t = a_t * h_(t-1) + b_t * x_t`, with
`a_t = sigmoid(x_t Wa)` (per-dimension decay in 0 to 1) and `b_t = x_t Wb`
(per-dimension input gate), then `y_t = h_t Wo` gated by the token. At
microscope scale the scan runs sequentially over the 28-position window;
`probes/c1_selective_scan_in_grad.mlpl` shows it traces through `grad`
and trains with `adam` today.

## What the microscope will measure

SS01: DN01 with attention replaced by the scan at matched parameters:
validation loss and family accuracy; the decay `a_t` per position on one
window (what the block forgets, drawn as a fading state chip); decode-time
bytes held per token for the state against the key-value cache attention
would hold, on the generation benchmark. SS02: the attention, state-space,
and MoE hybrid at several ratios, with the recurrence machinery for depth.

## What would demonstrate value

At matched parameters, the scan block within a small margin of attention's
validation loss with constant decode memory; and a hybrid ratio that keeps
attention's held-out MLPL answers (the first ones came from RC01 and RM01)
while the state-space blocks carry the rest at lower bytes per token.

## Status

Planned as Saga 7 (state-space-and-hybrid), next after the landscape:
SS01 simple, SS02 selective, HA01 with attention, SM01 with experts, LM01
latent experts. Nothing measured yet; the only evidence is the capability
probe.

## Deeper reference

  [`research4.txt`](../research/research4.txt)
- [Recurrence](recurrence.md) for the depth-without-parameters machinery
  the hybrid reuses

Demonstrated, with measurements: a dense baseline (DN01); top-1 and top-2
mixtures (MX01, MX02); measurable expert specialization; exact sparse
dispatch (SD01); the data-versus-epochs effect (DS01); low-rank delta
experts with a shared expert (LD01); an in-repo teacher fixture (TE01); the
resource budget (RB01) and a measured generation benchmark (GB01);
recurrence (RC01, RM01); the Engram table from scratch with exact parity
against the sw-MLPL builtin (EG01); all three sparsities together and the
seven-row ablation matrix (RE01); seven recordings replayed in the live
demo and handed to the generic Rust/Yew host; the campus docent's first
five steps (paused: it does not yet beat a deterministic matcher).

Still to come, in order: the landscape's acceptance pass (the animation
itself is live), a Mamba-style state-space block and the attention, state-space, and MoE
hybrid with latent experts, distillation, the state-memory-experts

   rank-4 delta experts cost 2,048 parameters against 4,288 for four full
   experts and give validation loss 3.46 with a shared always-on expert
   (the best non-recurrent row) and 3.79 without (the dense baseline's).
   Evidence: [LD01](docs/experiments/LD01.md).
7. **Reusing a block buys quality per parameter, and the router
   re-decides.** The mixture block applied three times with deep
   supervision reaches validation loss 3.42 at the same 7,096 parameters
   (MX01 3.76), and 38 to 46 percent of tokens change expert between
   recurrences. It is not a converging reasoning loop: the models score
   best when stopped early, and R=2 is worse than R=1. Evidence:
   [RC01](docs/experiments/RC01.md), [RM01](docs/experiments/RM01.md).
8. **External memory is memorization capacity at this data size.** The
   Engram table, written from scratch and equal to the sw-MLPL builtin to

"$mlpl" --source-dir "$repo_root" "$repo_root/demos/ssm_block.mlpl" -- "$tmp_rel" "$binary" "$mode"

if [ "$mode" = "write" ]; then
    cp "$repo_root/$tmp_rel/state-bytes-v0.json" "$repo_root/fixtures/ssm/state-bytes-v0.json"
fi

    generated="$repo_root/$tmp_rel/$name.svg"

    if [ "$mode" = "write" ]; then

        echo "$name.svg preview is stale; run scripts/run-ssm-demo write" >&2

# SS01: simple state-space block

## Question

Can a fixed-size state carry the sequence history instead of attention's
growing key-value cache, and what does that cost and buy at this scale?

## Change from the previous experiment

DN01's attention block is replaced by a diagonal linear state-space scan of
matched size: `s_t = a * s_(t-1) + x_t B`, `y_t = s_t C`, with the decay
`a = sigmoid(A)` learned per state dimension (32 logits), `B` a 16 by 32
projection, and `C` a 32 by 16 projection, followed by the same residual,
feed-forward block, norm, and head. Nothing else changes: the same
embedding, positions, window, split, epochs, learning rate, and masked
loss. The scan block has 1,056 parameters against attention's 1,024.

## Configuration

Embedding width 16, state width 32, hidden width 32; window 28; 120
examples (90 train, 30 validation); 300 epochs; Adam at learning rate
0.003; one process. The scan is written as one `repeat` per position and
traces through `grad` (probe C1); it is sequential by construction, with no
parallel scan. About a minute on a laptop, deterministic, so the diagrams,
the state-bytes fixture, and the results row are checked in the gate.

## Results

| Metric | SS01 | DN01 | Source |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Parameters | 3,844 | 3,812 | results rows |
| Sequence-mixer parameters | 1,056 | 1,024 | ssm-structure diagram |
| Active parameters per token | 3,028 | 2,996 | results rows |
| Validation masked loss | 4.56 | 3.79 | results rows |
| Perplexity | 95.8 | 44.2 | results rows |
| Held-out exact match: arith / seq / mlpl / prose | 0 / 0 / 0.286 / 0.667 | 0 / 0 / 0 / 0.667 | results rows |
| Training exact match | 0.99 | 0.70 | recordings (`accuracy/train`) |
| Best validation loss along the run | 1.96 at epoch 25 | 1.94 at epoch 25 | recordings |
| Interpreter time per training token | 0.023 ms | 0.020 ms | results rows (machine-dependent) |
| Persistent state at 16 / 1,024 tokens of history | 256 / 256 B | 4,096 / 262,144 B | results rows, last column |
| Learned decay, min / mean / max | 0.26 / 0.76 / 0.98 | - | `ssm/decay` |

Persistent state and prefill cost against history length, from
[`fixtures/ssm/state-bytes-v0.json`](../../fixtures/ssm/state-bytes-v0.json)
(bytes are derived from shapes, D; microseconds are measured on one
machine with `mlpl-repl 0.22.0`, M):

| History (tokens) | Attention K,V bytes | Scan state bytes | Attention us/token | Scan us/token |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 16 | 4,096 | 256 | 2.3 | 17.7 |
| 64 | 16,384 | 256 | 10.7 | 17.2 |
| 256 | 65,536 | 256 | 7.5 | 22.5 |
| 1,024 | 262,144 | 256 | 16.0 | 42.3 |

![SS01 structure: the window through embedding, the B projection, the diagonal scan with its 32-value state, the C projection, the residual, the FFN, norm, and head, with parameter counts, the learned decay strip, and the persistent-state table](../../assets/previews/ssm-structure.svg)

![SS01 window: the example 2+3=|5. with the argmax beside the target, a chip per position whose opacity is the share of that position surviving in the final state, and the 32-value state at every position](../../assets/previews/ssm-window.svg)

![SS01 state bytes against history: attention's key and value rows grow linearly from 4,096 to 262,144 bytes while the scan holds 256 bytes at every length; the table beside gives the measured microseconds per token](../../assets/previews/ssm-bytes.svg)

## What we learned

A 256-byte state learned this domain about as well as attention on the
training rows (exact match 0.99 against 0.70) and worse on the held-out
rows (validation loss 4.56 against 3.79, the same prose answers, one more
held-out MLPL answer). The block memorizes at least as readily: its
validation loss bottoms out at the same first checkpoint as DN01's and then
climbs higher. The learned decay spreads from 0.26 to 0.98 with mean 0.76,
so by the end of a seven-token window about a third of the first position
is still present in the state; the block keeps a soft summary, not an
exact record.

The memory claim holds exactly and by construction: the scan keeps 256
bytes of sequence state at any history while one-head attention keeps 256
bytes per token of history, 262,144 bytes at 1,024 tokens. The speed claim
does not hold in this interpreter: the sequential scan costs 17 to 42
microseconds per token of prefill against 2 to 16 for attention, because
each position is one interpreter step and attention is one matmul over the
window. Both numbers are stated in the diagram and the fixture.

This is [finding 11](../results/current-findings.md).

## What we did not prove

That a state-space block cannot match attention here: one seed, one state
width, 90 training windows, and a decay initialized at 0.9. Whether
input-dependent gating (SS02) or a single attention block among state
blocks (HA01) recovers the held-out loss is the next question. Nothing
here says anything about a compiled scan's speed.

## Raw evidence

```sh
just ssm             # run SS01 and check its diagrams, fixture, and results row
just ssm write       # regenerate the diagrams, re-measure the fixture, and rewrite the SS01 row
just recordings write SS01   # recapture the recording over mlpl-serve
```

Code: [`lib/ssm.mlpl`](../../lib/ssm.mlpl),
[`demos/ssm_block.mlpl`](../../demos/ssm_block.mlpl), tests
[`tests/test_ssm.mlpl`](../../tests/test_ssm.mlpl). Recording:
[`fixtures/recordings/state-space-run-v0.json`](../../fixtures/recordings/state-space-run-v0.json)
(13 frames; the last carries the decay, the state and survival along one
window, the argmax, and the byte accounting). Rows: SS01 and DN01 in the
[results table](../reference/results.md).

Attention carries context by keeping every earlier token's key and value,
so decode memory grows with the window and every new token reads all of
it. A state-space block (Mamba, Mamba-2) carries context in a fixed-size
state that is updated once per token and decays selectively: memory per

keep and what to forget. NVIDIA's Nemotron-H and Nemotron 3 Nano interleave
such blocks with a few attention blocks and MoE feed-forward blocks, keeping
attention's exact recall where it matters and constant-memory context
everywhere else.

## Basic idea

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  x[token x_t] --> b[x_t B]
  h0[state s_t-1] --> u[s_t = a * s_t-1 + x_t B]
  b --> u
  a[decay a = sigmoid A] --> u
  u --> o[s_t C]
  o --> y[y_t into the residual stream]
```

The simple block (SS01) written out: `s_t = a * s_(t-1) + x_t B` and
`y_t = s_t C`, with `a = sigmoid(A)` a learned decay per state dimension
held in 0 to 1, and `B`, `C` small projections. The selective block (SS02)
makes the decay and the input gate functions of the token: `a_t =
sigmoid(x_t Wa)`, `b_t = x_t Wb`. At microscope scale the scan runs
sequentially over the 28-position window as one `repeat` per position;
`probes/c1_selective_scan_in_grad.mlpl` shows the form traces through
`grad` and trains with `adam`, and `lib/ssm.mlpl` is the lesson's version.

## What the microscope measured

SS01 is DN01 with attention replaced by the simple scan at matched size
(1,056 parameters against 1,024), trained with the DN01 budget:

| | SS01 scan | DN01 attention |
|---|---:|---:|
| Validation loss | 4.56 | 3.79 |
| Held-out exact match, arith / seq / mlpl / prose | 0 / 0 / 0.286 / 0.667 | 0 / 0 / 0 / 0.667 |
| Training exact match | 0.99 | 0.70 |
| Persistent state at 1,024 tokens of history | 256 B | 262,144 B |
| Prefill, microseconds per token at 1,024 tokens (interpreter) | 42.3 | 16.0 |

The learned decay spans 0.26 to 0.98 (mean 0.76): about a third of the
first position of a seven-token window is still in the state at its end.

diagrams (structure and bytes, the state along one window as fading chips,
state bytes against history).

at least as well as attention (better exact match, lower training loss)
and generalized worse (validation loss 4.56 against 3.79, the same prose
answers, one more MLPL answer). What it costs: nothing in memory, exactly

token, because a sequential scan is one interpreter step per position
while attention is one matmul over the window.

attention's held-out MLPL answers (the first ones came from RC01 and RM01)
while the state-space blocks carry the rest at lower bytes per token. SS01
delivers the constant memory and not the margin; SS02 (selective gating)
and HA01 (one attention block among state blocks) are the next two rows.

1	# Concepts
2	
3	A visual learning path. Each step adds one mechanism and asks one
4	question; each page answers what problem the mechanism solves, the basic
5	idea, what the microscope measures, what would demonstrate value, and
6	which experiments exist. Pages read front to back in this order.
7	
8	```mermaid
9	flowchart LR
10	  A[1 Dense model] --> B[2 Add experts]
11	  B --> C[3 Route to top-k]
12	  C --> D[4 Skip inactive experts]
13	  D --> E[5 Reuse one block recursively]
14	  E --> F[6 Add Engram memory]
15	  F --> G[7 Quantize experts]
16	  G --> H[8 Keep only hot experts resident]
17	  H --> I[9 Schedule across CPU and NPU]
18	```
19	
20	| Step | Question | Page | Status |
21	|---|---|---|---|
22	| 1 | How good is a tiny dense model? | [Dense versus MoE](dense-vs-moe.md) | measured (DN01) |
23	| 2, 3 | Can we store more model than we execute, and what does the second expert cost? | [Routing and top-k](routing.md) | measured (MX01, MX02) |
24	| 4 | Can conditional compute actually avoid the unused work? | [Sparse dispatch](sparse-dispatch.md) | measured (SD01, GB01) |
25	| 2b | How many experts can we afford? | [Low-rank delta experts](delta-experts.md) | measured (LD01) |
26	| 5 | Can compute replace parameters? | [Recurrence](recurrence.md) | measured (RC01, RM01) |
27	| 6 | Can cheap lookup memory replace learned memorization? | [Engram](engram.md) | measured (EG01, RE01) |
28	| 6b | Can a teacher improve a tiny student? | [Distillation](distillation.md) | teacher fixture exists (TE01) |
29	| 7 | How many experts fit in the same storage? | [Quantization](quantization.md) | projected (RB01) |
30	| 8 | Does the whole model need to be resident? | [Expert cache](expert-cache.md) | estimated (RB01) |
31	| 9 | Should every expert run on the same device? | [Heterogeneous execution](heterogeneous-execution.md) | planned |
32	| 10 | Can a state-space block replace attention, and does a hybrid keep the best of each? | [State-space block](state-space.md) | measured (SS01: constant 256 B state, validation loss 4.56 against 3.79); SS02 and HA01 next |
33	
34	## Resource allocation axes
35	
36	The four sparsities the project started with, extended by
37	[`research4.txt`](../research/research4.txt) to the axes a tiny model on a
38	small CPU has to allocate; each has, or will have, a lesson that turns it
39	on alone against the dense baseline.
40	
41	| Axis | The question it answers | Mechanism | Where it is measured |
42	|---|---|---|---|
43	| Compute | which computation executes? | top-k routing and sparse dispatch | MX01, MX02, SD01 |
44	| Parameters | how many transformations share weights? | recurrence | RC01, RM01, RE01 (measured) |
45	| Memory | what can be retrieved instead of recomputed? | Engram | EG01, RE01 (measured; not yet valuable at 90 windows) |
46	| State | how much sequence history stays resident? | state-space block | SS01 (measured: 256 B at any history against 262,144 B for attention at 1,024 tokens); SS02, HA01 (Saga 7) |
47	| Residency | what must be in fast memory right now? | expert cache | XC01 (planned); RB01 gives the estimates |
48	| Precision | how many bits represent each parameter? | quantization | QZ01 (planned); RB01 projects |
49	| Time | how many future tokens can one state predict? | multi-token prediction | MT01 to MT03 (planned, Saga 10) |
50	
51	## The parts and why they exist
52	
53	| Part | Job | Why it matters |
54	|---|---|---|
55	| Router | chooses experts per token | activates only useful capacity |
56	| Experts | learn different transformations | raise stored capacity |
57	| Top-k | sets experts used per token | the quality-versus-compute knob |
58	| Load balancing | prevents expert collapse | keeps capacity usable |
59	| Sparse dispatch | runs only selected experts | turns sparsity into less work |
60	| Recurrence | reuses one block several times | more computation without more parameters |
61	| State-space block | carries the context in a fixed-size state that decays per token | constant memory per token during decode; attention kept only where recall needs it |
62	| Engram | retrieves memorized n-gram information | moves lookup-like knowledge out of weights |
63	| Distillation | transfers behavior from a larger model | improves tiny-model quality |
64	| Quantization | shrinks expert representation | lets more experts fit in memory |
65	| Expert cache | keeps hot experts in fast memory | lets the model exceed fast memory |
66	| CPU/NPU scheduling | sends work where it fits | exploits heterogeneous hardware |
67	| Packed model | bounded inference artifact | tests whether the design fits constrained devices |
68	
69	Metrics are grouped the same way everywhere: quality (exact match by task
70	family and overall), model economics (total and active parameters, bytes
71	per token), runtime (expert evaluations, cache hits, latency), and
72	diagnostics (loss, perplexity, entropy, KL, balance).

**What landed** (commit 53a8c1e, metadata in f5dfc2b, both on `main`):

- **The block.** `lib/ssm.mlpl` writes the diagonal linear scan out, with a learned per-dimension decay held in 0 to 1 by a sigmoid and two small projections. The scan is one `repeat` per position and traces through `grad` with a runtime count.
- **The lesson.** `demos/ssm_block.mlpl` is DN01 with attention swapped for the scan at matched size, trained on the same budget in one process. It records the decay, the state along one window, how much of each position survives to the window's end, the argmax, and the byte accounting.
- **The results column.** The table gains a last column for persistent state bytes at 16 and 1,024 tokens of history, filled for DN01 and SS01 and dashed elsewhere.
- **Visuals and docs, as you asked.** Three diagrams (structure and decay, fading state chips along one window, state bytes against history with measured microseconds), a pinned recording replayed in the live demo and verified headlessly, the catalog entry, the SS01 report, the concept page with measured numbers, finding 11, a report-card entry, the host handoff's new shapes, and README claim 10.

| Measure | SS01 scan | DN01 attention |
|---|---:|---:|
| Validation loss | 4.56 | 3.79 |
| Training exact match | 0.99 | 0.70 |

The memory claim holds exactly. The fixed state memorizes more and generalizes less than attention here, and the sequential scan is slower in the interpreter. Both numbers are stated in the diagram and the pinned fixture.

content.content:
#!/bin/sh
set -eu

# Gate check: docs/mlplcode.org must reproduce every source it explains.
# Tangle rule (the same one org-babel-tangle applies): for each
# `#+begin_src <lang> :tangle <path>` block, in document order, the block
# body is appended to <path> (relative to docs/) with one blank line between
# blocks. Implemented in awk so the check needs no Emacs; when Emacs is
# available the same tangle is also run through org-babel-tangle and must
# agree.
repo_dir=$(CDPATH= cd -- "$(dirname -- "$0")/.." && pwd)
org=$repo_dir/docs/mlplcode.org
# Scratch lives under the ignored ./work directory, never /tmp.
work=$repo_dir/work/tangle-awk.$$
rm -rf "$work"; mkdir -p "$work"
trap 'rm -rf "$work"' EXIT

awk -v out="$work" '
/^#\+begin_src / {
    target = ""
    for (i = 2; i <= NF; i++) if ($i == ":tangle") target = $(i + 1)
    if (target != "" && target != "no") {
        sub(/^\.\.\//, "", target)
        file = out "/" target
        dir = file; sub(/\/[^\/]*$/, "", dir)
        system("mkdir -p \"" dir "\"")
        if (file in seen) printf "\n" >> file
        seen[file] = 1
        inblock = 1
        next
    }
}
/^#\+end_src/ { inblock = 0; next }
inblock { print >> file }
' "$org"

status=0
count=0
for tangled in $(cd "$work" && find . -type f | sort); do
    rel=${tangled#./}
    count=$((count + 1))
    if ! cmp -s "$work/$rel" "$repo_dir/$rel"; then
        echo "tangle drift: docs/mlplcode.org does not reproduce $rel" >&2
        diff "$repo_dir/$rel" "$work/$rel" | head -20 >&2
        status=1
    fi
done
[ "$count" -gt 0 ] || { echo "no tangle targets found in docs/mlplcode.org" >&2; exit 1; }

emacs=${EMACS:-}
[ -n "$emacs" ] || command -v emacs >/dev/null 2>&1 && emacs=${emacs:-emacs} || true
[ -n "$emacs" ] || [ ! -x /Applications/Emacs.app/Contents/MacOS/Emacs ] || emacs=/Applications/Emacs.app/Contents/MacOS/Emacs
if [ -n "$emacs" ]; then
    ework=$repo_dir/work/tangle-emacs.$$
    rm -rf "$ework"; mkdir -p "$ework/docs"
    cp "$org" "$ework/docs/mlplcode.org"
    # org-babel-tangle does not create target directories.
    for tangled in $(cd "$work" && find . -type f | sort); do
        mkdir -p "$ework/$(dirname "${tangled#./}")"
    done
    if "$emacs" --batch -l org --eval "(progn (add-to-list 'org-babel-tangle-lang-exts '(\"mlpl\" . \"mlpl\")) (org-babel-tangle-file \"$ework/docs/mlplcode.org\"))" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
        for tangled in $(cd "$work" && find . -type f | sort); do
            rel=${tangled#./}
            cmp -s "$ework/$rel" "$repo_dir/$rel" || { echo "org-babel-tangle differs from the committed $rel" >&2; status=1; }
        done
        echo "tangle: $count files reproduced by awk and by org-babel-tangle ($emacs)"
    else
        echo "tangle: $count files reproduced by awk; org-babel-tangle failed to run, see $ework" >&2
    fi
    [ "$status" -eq 0 ] && rm -rf "$ework"
else
    echo "tangle: $count files reproduced by awk (no Emacs found to cross-check)"
fi
exit "$status"
=== mlplcode.org 60-130
  asked, or to a function to decide per block.
- To evaluate every runnable block at once use =C-c C-v C-b=
  (~org-babel-execute-buffer~); blocks marked ~:eval no-export~ or
  ~:eval never~ are skipped, so that command runs only the primer examples.

** Publishing

~just publish-doc~ writes ~out/docs/mlplcode.{html,txt,md,pdf}~ with Emacs
in batch mode and, for the PDF, Chrome headless; nothing is evaluated and
nothing is installed. The same exports are available interactively from
=C-c C-e=.

** Regenerating the sources

~just tangle~ runs org-babel-tangle over this file and then the drift
check; ~just tangle-check~ runs only the check.

* MLPL in ten minutes

The language is small and the agent uses a small part of it.

- *Values.* Numbers, strings, string lists such as ~["a", "b"]~, and records
  such as ~{tool: "read", path: "src/lib.mlpl"}~. Records are immutable
  values; to change one, build a new one. A field is read with a dot:
  ~action.tool~.
- *Functions.* ~def u:name(a, b) { "docstring"; body }~. The ~u:~ prefix
  marks a user-defined function. The first expression is a docstring. The
  last expression is the return value; there is no ~return~ keyword and no
  early return, which is why the code nests ~if~ ... ~else~ instead of
  returning early, and why a six-way choice is a six-deep chain (there is no
  ~else if~ or ~match~).
- *Results.* Anything that can fail answers ~ok(value)~ or ~err(message)~.
  ~is_ok~, ~is_err~, ~unwrap~, ~unwrap_or~, and ~err_message~ take them
  apart. Writing ~?~ after an expression inside a function means: if this is
  an ~err~, return it from the function now. That is the only early exit.
- *Function references.* ~:u:name~ is a reference to a function.
  ~call(f, x)~ invokes one. Calling with fewer arguments than the function
  takes returns a partial, a value that remembers the bound arguments and
  behaves like a smaller function. The agent's model, decision, and verify
  hooks are all passed this way.
- *Loops.* ~while cond { ... }~ with ~break~. ~if~ is an expression, so
  ~x = if c { a } else { b }~ is common.
- *Strings.* ~str_concat~, ~str_join(list, sep)~, ~str_split~, ~str_find~
  (index or -1), ~str_slice(s, start, len)~, ~str_len~, ~str_eq~. String
  lists are read with ~list_len~ and ~list_get~ (which answers a Result).
  The code joins strings with ~str_concat~ and ~str_join~ rather than ~+~
  because when it was written ~+~ rejected strings; that has since been
  fixed upstream.
- *Files.* ~read_text~, ~write_atomic~, ~fs_walk~, ~run_script~ are all
  confined to a sandbox root given on the command line and answer Results.
- *Modules.* ~include "file.mlpl"~ splices another file in, resolved
  relative to the including file. A binding made at the top level of a file
  is visible inside functions that run later, which the tools module uses
  for the extension root.

** Try it: Results and ~?~

These three blocks are self-contained and safe to evaluate.

#+begin_src mlpl :tangle no :exports both
def u:half(n) {
  "Half of a non-negative number, or an err naming the problem.";
  if n < 0 { err("negative: " + to_string(n)) } else { ok(n / 2) }
}

def u:quarter(n) {
  "Half of half; the ? returns the first err as this function's value.";
  h = u:half(n)?;
  u:half(h)
}

=== tangle block sample

* How the model is injected: =agents/model.mlpl=

A model is anything you can call with one prompt string and get one reply string back. Keeping that shape lets a test substitute a fixed reply for a live server, which is why nothing in the loop knows whether it is talking to Ollama.

** Module header

#+begin_src mlpl :tangle ../agents/model.mlpl
# Model injection: every agent takes a one-argument ask function; these are the standard ones.
#+end_src

** =u:ask_live=

~llm_call~ is the language builtin that posts to an Ollama server. Binding the first three arguments with ~call(:u:ask_live, host, model, system)~ yields a partial, a plain value that behaves like a one-argument function. The entries build the live model this way.

#+begin_src mlpl :tangle ../agents/model.mlpl
def u:ask_live(host, model, system, prompt) {
  "Ask a live Ollama model; bind host, model, and system with call() to get a one-argument ask.";
  llm_call(host, prompt, model, system)
}
#+end_src

** =u:ask_scripted=

* MLPL in ten minutes

The language is small and the agent uses a small part of it.

- *Values.* Numbers, strings, string lists such as ~["a", "b"]~, and records
  such as ~{tool: "read", path: "src/lib.mlpl"}~. Records are immutable
  values; to change one, build a new one. A field is read with a dot:
  ~action.tool~.
- *Functions.* ~def u:name(a, b) { "docstring"; body }~. The ~u:~ prefix
  marks a user-defined function. The first expression is a docstring. The
  last expression is the return value; there is no ~return~ keyword and no
  early return, which is why the code nests ~if~ ... ~else~ instead of
  returning early, and why a six-way choice is a six-deep chain (there is no
  ~else if~ or ~match~).
- *Results.* Anything that can fail answers ~ok(value)~ or ~err(message)~.
  ~is_ok~, ~is_err~, ~unwrap~, ~unwrap_or~, and ~err_message~ take them
  apart. Writing ~?~ after an expression inside a function means: if this is
  an ~err~, return it from the function now. That is the only early exit.
- *Function references.* ~:u:name~ is a reference to a function.
  ~call(f, x)~ invokes one. Calling with fewer arguments than the function
  takes returns a partial, a value that remembers the bound arguments and
  behaves like a smaller function. The agent's model, decision, and verify
  hooks are all passed this way.
- *Loops.* ~while cond { ... }~ with ~break~. ~if~ is an expression, so
  ~x = if c { a } else { b }~ is common.
- *Strings.* ~str_concat~, ~str_join(list, sep)~, ~str_split~, ~str_find~
  (index or -1), ~str_slice(s, start, len)~, ~str_len~, ~str_eq~. String
  lists are read with ~list_len~ and ~list_get~ (which answers a Result).
  The code joins strings with ~str_concat~ and ~str_join~ rather than ~+~
  because when it was written ~+~ rejected strings; that has since been
  fixed upstream.
- *Files.* ~read_text~, ~write_atomic~, ~fs_walk~, ~run_script~ are all
  confined to a sandbox root given on the command line and answer Results.
- *Modules.* ~include "file.mlpl"~ splices another file in, resolved
  relative to the including file. A binding made at the top level of a file
  is visible inside functions that run later, which the tools module uses
  for the extension root.
